newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Boeing latest in long line of EU/U.S trade disputes.
newsitem.headline: Boeing latest in long line of EU/U.S trade disputes.

text.p: If there was a theme tune for trade relations between the EU and U.S., Gershwin's "Lets call the whole thing off" would be an appropriate refrain.
Written in 1937, the song highlights the differences between Americans and Britons with a play on the pronounciation of words such as "tomato" and "potato", "either" and "neither".
While London's "special relationship" with Washington is now overtaken -- on trade matters at least -- by links at U.S./EU level, these fundamental differences remain.
The latest discord stems from the European Commission's determination to block a merger between U.S. Boeing Corp and McDonnell Douglas Corp unless Boeing meets its objections.
It is just the latest in a long list of squabbles that have soured transatlantic relations in the last 18 months.
"We could be heading for a major trade war with the EU over this," said U.S. Congressman Norman Dicks who has hundreds of Boeing workers in his Washington State constituency.
The EU demurs. "This is not a trade issue," said European Commission spokesman Willy Helin. "This is a competitions question."

U.S. President Bill Clinton entered the fray later on Thursday saying: "There is an orderly process for our handling of this and I think we'd better let the orderly process play itself out before we talk ourselves into a trade war."

"There are fundemental differences of opinion between the EU and U.S. on what constitutes free trade, free market, even free spiritedness," a Brussels-based lawyer specialising in global trade told Reuters.
"I am often very surprised at how utterly bewildered Americans and Europeans can be when it comes to trying to understand the other point of view."
The "New Transatlantic Agenda" launched in 1994 was supposed to showcase links between the U.S. and EU -- the strongest and most important trading partnership in the world.

Since then -- and despite countless industry committees established to try to avoid the kind of public laundry-washing likely to emerge in the wake of the Boeing row -- Washington has argued with the EU on topics ranging from Cuba to the Internet.
The Cuba row was on Wednesday put on the back-burner for at least another six months when Clinton extended waivers on certain parts of the Helms-Burton Act for at least another six months.

This U.S. law has been one of the most testing transatlantic trade disputes in decades. Europeans saw it as unacceptable meddling by Washington, prohibiting EU companies from legitimately carrying out business in Cuba.
On their part, scores of Washington politicians have been utterly unable to comprehend how anyone else could not see the threat posed to the U.S. by Cuba or by helping Cuba survive.

But striking differences have also emerged between the U.S. and EU over efforts to globalise financial services trade and also how governments should -- or should not -- regulate the increase in Internet-related commerce.

Despite trumpeting EU/U.S. cooperation as a model for global trade ties, the EU's Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan has spent more time on the U.S. side of the Atlantic this year than in any other country.

The European Commission says this proves the "constant dialogue" policy works -- albeit that the Helms-Burton row was only resolved the last minute before it went to a World Trade Organisation disputes panel.
Since 1994 there have also been furious rows over semi-conductor trade, car exports, alcohol sales and media mergers.
The Boeing story seems to be following a similar pattern -- business complaints followed by government intervention followed by stand-off followed by resolution.

"I suspect a satisfactory conclusion to the Boeing merger will emerge," said the trade lawyer. "I don't think it will be thrashed out between Boeing and the EU ... I suspect it will be between Washington and the Commission.
